title: 资源分配与阶段检查 · Four listening sections
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。四节音频共40题，按顺序听音作答。合成训练音频时长不同于正式考试。
transcript:
Section 1: Community Garden Planning Meeting

Mia: Hi, thanks for coming to the community garden meeting. I'm Mia, the volunteer coordinator. 
Ben: Nice to meet you, Mia. I'm Ben. I heard you need help with the new garden plan. 
Mia: Yes, we do. So, first, let's talk about resources. We have a small budget this year—only 500 dollars. 
Ben: 500 dollars? That's not much. How do you want to spend it? 
Mia: Well, we need seeds and tools. Last year we spent 200 dollars on seeds, but this year seeds are cheaper. We can buy seeds for 150 dollars. 
Ben: OK, 150 for seeds. What about tools? 
Mia: We already have some tools, but we need two new spades. Each spade costs 25 dollars. 
Ben: So that's 50 dollars for spades. And the rest? 
Mia: We also need to fix the water pipe. The repair will cost 100 dollars. 
Ben: Wait, let me add that up. 150 plus 50 is 200, plus 100 is 300. So we have 200 dollars left. 
Mia: Yes, exactly. We can use that for plants—maybe some fruit trees. 
Ben: Good idea. Now, about the schedule. When do we start planting? 
Mia: We planned to start on April 15th, but the weather might be cold. So we moved it to April 22nd. 
Ben: April 22nd. That's a Saturday, right? 
Mia: Yes, it's a Saturday. And we need volunteers. Can you help on that day? 
Ben: I can help in the morning, but I have a class in the afternoon. 
Mia: That's fine. We need people from 9 to 12. 
Ben: OK, I'll be there at 9. Oh, and one more thing—who is going to lead the planting? 
Mia: Sarah will lead it. She has a lot of experience. 
Ben: Sarah? I thought she was away in May. 
Mia: No, she's away in June, not May. So she can help in April. 
Ben: Great. And what about the tools we already have? Are they in good condition? 
Mia: Some are, but the old wheelbarrow is broken. We need to buy a new one. It costs 80 dollars. 
Ben: Wait, that changes the budget. So now we have 200 minus 80, which is 120 dollars left. 
Mia: Right. So we can't buy fruit trees this year. We'll just buy seeds and maybe some small plants. 
Ben: OK, that makes sense. So the total spending is 150 for seeds, 50 for spades, 100 for pipe repair, and 80 for wheelbarrow. That's 380 dollars. 
Mia: Yes, and we have 120 dollars left for small plants. 
Ben: Good. Now, about the stages—when do we check progress? 
Mia: We'll have a check-in meeting on May 10th to see how the plants are growing. 
Ben: May 10th. And who will be there? 
Mia: All volunteers, including you, if you can come. 
Ben: I'll try. Also, do we need to bring anything? 
Mia: Yes, please bring your own gloves. We don't have enough for everyone. 
Ben: Got it. Gloves. And what about water? 
Mia: We have a tap, but if the pipe repair isn't done, we'll need to bring water bottles. 
Ben: OK. I think that's everything. Thanks, Mia. 
Mia: Thank you, Ben. See you on April 22nd.

Section 2: Community Garden Meeting: Allocating Resources and Checking Progress

Hello everyone, and thanks for coming to the monthly meeting of the Green Lane Community Garden. I'm Sarah, the volunteer coordinator. I'm glad to see so many familiar faces here today, and I appreciate everyone taking the time to join us. Today we need to talk about resource allocation and check our progress on the new herb garden. We have several important points to cover, so let's begin.

First, let's look at the budget. We have £500 left for this year. Last month we spent £200 on seeds and tools. So, if we buy the new water tank for £150, we will have £150 remaining for other things. But remember, we also need to pay for the insurance in December, which costs £100. So, if we buy the tank now, we might not have enough for insurance. We need to decide carefully, so please think about this before we vote. This is a decision that affects the whole garden, so I want everyone to feel they understand the numbers before we make a choice together.

Second, volunteers. We have 12 active volunteers, but only 5 can come on Saturdays. If we want to finish the herb garden by October, we need more help on weekends. Please talk to your friends. If each volunteer brings one friend, we will have enough people. This is very important for our plans, because without enough hands on Saturdays, the work will take much longer than we hope.

Now, progress check. The herb garden was started in May. We have planted 20 herb plants so far: 8 basil, 6 mint, and 6 rosemary. The basil is growing well, but the mint is not doing so well because it gets too much sun. We need to move the mint to a shadier spot. Also, the rosemary needs more water. If we water it twice a day, it will probably recover. Please help with this when you can, even if it is only for a few minutes during your visit.

Next, the compost area. We built three compost bins in June. They are working well, but we need more brown material, like dry leaves. If you have dry leaves at home, please bring them. This will help our compost and our garden, and it is an easy way for everyone to contribute something useful.

Finally, events. We are planning a garden open day on September 15th. We need volunteers to help with setting up stalls and guiding visitors. If we have at least 10 volunteers, the event will run smoothly. Please sign up on the sheet by the door.

Thank you for listening. Let's work together to make our garden even better.

Section 3: Resource Allocation and Stage Check: A Student-Tutor Meeting

Tutor: Good morning, Mei and Daniel. Thanks for coming. Let's review your project on resource allocation for the community garden. Mei, can you start with the stage check?
Mei: Yes. We've finished the planning stage. We allocated the budget last week. We decided to spend 60 percent on tools and seeds, and 40 percent on soil and compost.
Daniel: Actually, Mei, we changed that. Remember? After the meeting with the garden committee, we agreed to spend 50 percent on tools and seeds, 30 percent on soil, and 20 percent on a water tank.
Mei: Oh right, sorry. Yes, 50, 30, and 20. The water tank is important because the dry season is coming.
Tutor: Good. So the allocation is now 50-30-20. What about the timeline? Have you set any checkpoints?
Daniel: We have two checkpoints. The first is at the end of this month, when we'll check if the tools have arrived. The second is in six weeks, when we'll check the water tank installation.
Tutor: And what will you do if the tools are late?
Mei: If the tools are late, we will borrow some from the community center. That way, we can start planting on time.
Tutor: That's a good contingency. Now, about the budget: you mentioned 20 percent for the water tank. Is that enough?
Daniel: We think so. But if the tank costs more, we will reduce the soil budget. We won't reduce the tools budget because we need them for planting.
Tutor: I see. So the priority is tools, then water, then soil. Is that correct?
Mei: Yes, that's right. Tools are essential. Water is also essential, but we can delay the tank if necessary. Soil is the most flexible.
Tutor: Good. Now, let's talk about the stage check report. When will you submit it?
Daniel: We plan to submit it next Friday. But we have a problem: the report needs data from the committee, and they haven't sent it yet.
Tutor: Have you asked them?
Mei: Yes, we emailed them yesterday. If they don't reply by Wednesday, we will call them.
Tutor: Good. And what about the presentation? Will you present together?
Daniel: Yes, we will. Mei will talk about the budget, and I will talk about the timeline. We will also show the water tank plan.
Tutor: That sounds fine. One more thing: the committee asked for a risk assessment. Have you included that?
Mei: Not yet. But we will add a short section. If we have time, we will also include a map of the garden.
Tutor: The risk assessment is more important. Focus on that first. So, to summarize: the allocation is 50-30-20, two checkpoints, a contingency for late tools, and a risk assessment to add. Is that everything?
Daniel: Yes, I think so. We'll send you the draft by Thursday.
Tutor: Perfect. Thank you both.

Section 4: Allocating Resources and Checking Progress: A Lecture on Project Management

Good morning, everyone. Today we'll look at two connected ideas in project management: resource allocation and stage checks. These are important for any project, whether you're building a bridge or organising a small event. Understanding how these two ideas work together will help you manage projects more effectively, no matter how big or small they are. These ideas apply in every kind of organisation, from large construction companies to small community groups, so the principles we discuss today are useful in many different situations. Whether you are a manager, a team member, or a volunteer, you will meet these ideas in your work.

Let's start with resource allocation. This means deciding how to use your resources—money, time, people, and equipment—across different tasks. A common mistake is to give too many resources to one part of the project and not enough to another. For example, if you spend most of your budget on marketing at the beginning, you might not have enough for production later. So, how do you allocate resources well? First, you need a clear plan. You should list all tasks and estimate what each one needs. Second, you should prioritise. Not all tasks are equally important. You need to identify the critical ones that must be finished on time. Third, you should review your allocation regularly. Things change, and what seemed enough last month may not be enough now.

Now, let's move on to stage checks. A stage check is a planned review at the end of a phase in the project. It helps you see if you are on track. There are three main questions to ask at a stage check. First, have we completed the planned work? Second, have we stayed within budget? Third, are there any new risks? If the answer to any of these is no, you may need to adjust your plan. Stage checks also help with communication. They give the team a chance to share progress and problems. Without regular checks, small issues can become big problems. For instance, if you don't check your spending, you might overspend without noticing. So, stage checks are not just about looking back; they are also about planning forward.

In summary, good resource allocation and regular stage checks are essential for project success. They help you use your resources wisely and keep the project on track. Thank you for listening. Next week, we'll look at how to handle changes in project scope.

grammar.title: 条件句；数量词；段落间的指代与衔接
grammar.explanation: 条件句用if引导，表示假设；数量词如some, any, much, many表示数量；指代与衔接用代词（如it, they）和连接词（如but, so）使段落连贯。
grammar.example: If the pipe repair isn't done, we'll need to bring water bottles.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word: If it rains tomorrow, we ______ stay at home.
questions.explanation: 条件句表示将来可能的情况，主句用will。
questions.evidence: If the pipe repair isn't done, we'll need to bring water bottles.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word: There aren't ______ chairs for everyone.
questions.explanation: enough表示足够，修饰名词chairs。
questions.evidence: We don't have enough for everyone.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct pronoun: The wheelbarrow is broken. ______ needs to be fixed.
questions.explanation: wheelbarrow是单数事物，用it指代。
questions.evidence: the old wheelbarrow is broken. We need to buy a new one.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct connector: We have 120 dollars left, ______ we can't buy fruit trees.
questions.explanation: so表示结果，前后是因果关系。
questions.evidence: So we can't buy fruit trees this year.
